notes.448: Line 456: Tento is read as vento (“wind”). Lines 462 and 461 stand in this order in the text as given and are translated in that order.

nodes.text: Whatever feeds grief, think it too much.
Nurse.
Has your love for glorious Alcides fled from you?
Deianira.
It has not fled, nurse; it stays, and sits deep,
fixed in my marrow, believe me; but a great pain
is love enraged.
Nurse.
By magic arts, as a rule,
wives bind their marriages, with prayers mixed in.
I have ordered a grove to break into spring in the midst of the cold,
and a hurled thunderbolt to stand still; I have stirred up the strait
when the wind was dropping; I have smoothed out a troubled sea,
and the dry earth has opened with new springs;
rocks have moved. I have shattered the doors
and the darkness of Dis, and, commanded by my prayer,
the dead speak. The hound of the underworld has fallen silent;
midnight has seen the sun, and day the night:
sea, earth, sky and Tartarus serve me,
and nothing keeps its laws against my chants:
we will bend him; my spells will find a way.
Deianira.
What herbs Pontus produces, or what Thessalian
Pindus nurtures beneath its crag: where shall I find a bane
to which he would yield? Though by a magic chant to earth
the Moon should come down, deserting the stars,
and winter see harvests, and at a chant the fleeting
thunderbolt stand caught, and, the order reversed,
midday blaze with the stars crowded in:
it will not bend him.
Nurse.
Love has conquered even the gods above.
